phase1.title: Phase 1 — In-Memory Data Engine

jvm-tuning.title: JVM build and start-up tuning (Track B)
jvm-tuning.goal:
Track B tuning task (identical for both JVM languages): your accepted engine is in `implementations/{{LANG_DIR}}/`. Tune its build and runtime for (1) start-up time (process spawn to first protocol response), (2) first-query (cold) latency and (3) warm query latency on the benchmark workload `benchmarks/workloads/analytics.json` at scale 1m (generate with `python3 datasets/generators/pqgen.py generate --scale 1m`), without changing results. Work through these areas and keep only changes whose effect you measured beyond run-to-run noise:

* **Compilation:** {{TUNING_NOTE}}
* **Boxing and dispatch in hot loops:** find and remove boxed arithmetic and boxed collections, reflective calls and avoidable dynamic dispatch in the execution, storage and value code. SQL overflow semantics stay exact: wherever `NUMERIC_OVERFLOW` must be raised, use checked operations (e.g. `Math.addExact`), never silently wrapping arithmetic.
* **JVM start-up:** a JDK AOT cache (JDK 27: `-XX:AOTCacheOutput` during `make build`, `-XX:AOTCache` in the launcher) or CDS. Any training run must use synthetic data and generic queries, never the benchmark queries. A stale or unusable cache must be ignored silently (stdout carries the protocol), and `make build` must still succeed if training fails.
* **JVM flags:** evaluate candidates one at a time (GC choice, heap sizing, `-XX:-UsePerfData`, code cache, pre-touch). Do not use `-XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1` (it trades steady-state speed for start-up). Report the memory (RSS) cost of each kept flag.

Measure before/after yourself through `bin/polyquery session` (start-up, first run and warm median per workload query) and report the results in README.md.
jvm-tuning.done: Conformance is unchanged: `python3 tests/conformance/runner.py --engine implementations/{{LANG_DIR}}/bin/polyquery` passes everything it passed before, as do `--modes`, `--transport http`, `--native native-kernels/build/x86_64/libpqkernels.so` (build the library with `make -C native-kernels`) and `python3 tests/concurrency/http_suite.py --engine implementations/{{LANG_DIR}}/bin/polyquery`; the capability set is unchanged; `make build test lint` succeed; README.md has a tuning section listing every technique tried as kept or dropped with its measured effect (start-up, cold, warm, RSS); `ENGINE.json` records the kept tuning; all work is committed.

fix-large-data.title: Defect fix — large data (10m rows) and memory exhaustion
fix-large-data.goal: Defect report (engine-specific): your accepted engine (Phases 1–5 and all later changes) is in `implementations/{{LANG_DIR}}/`. It cannot run the benchmark workload at 10 million rows. When the 9 tables of `benchmarks/workloads/analytics.json` are generated at scale 10m (`python3 datasets/generators/pqgen.py generate --scale 10m --jobs 8`, about 1.9 GB of CSV; the largest file, transactions.csv, is 0.87 GB) and loaded, the engine process dies while loading the first table, before any query runs, instead of answering. This violates the specification: an engine MUST NOT crash, hang or exit on any request, and out-of-memory conditions are reported as `RESOURCE_LIMIT` (`spec/errors/errors.md`); default ingestion limits allow at least 2 GiB of input and 200,000,000 rows (`spec/data-types/ingestion.md` §3); `--max-query-memory-mb` and `--max-ingest-bytes` are enforced with `RESOURCE_LIMIT` (`spec/sql/semantics.md` §15, `spec/protocol/protocol.md`). Fix the engine so that (1) the full 10m workload loads and all 20 queries answer correctly, and (2) when memory really runs out — e.g. many large tables loaded into one process — the request fails with `RESOURCE_LIMIT` and the engine keeps serving instead of dying. The host has ample memory (≈250 GB); a run that exceeds 120 GiB is stopped by the check. Keep all existing behaviour, capabilities and performance at smaller scales. The public check is `tests/regression/large_data_probe.py` (read its docstring: checks workload, query_budget, ingest_limit, exhaustion).

optimize-scaling.title: Optimization — scaling to 10m rows
optimize-scaling.goal: Performance problem report (engine-specific; no requirement change): your accepted engine (Phases 1–5 and all later changes) is in `implementations/{{LANG_DIR}}/`. It scales badly from 1 million to 10 million rows on the benchmark workload `benchmarks/workloads/analytics.json`, measured with the project's harness `benchmarks/harness/bench.py` (one session per engine: all nine tables loaded, the workload's two indexes created, then 3 warm-up and 7 measured rounds in which the 20 queries run in a random order per round; 16 CPUs). Geometric mean of the 20 per-query medians: 2.86 ms at 1m, 70.7 ms at 10m (24.8x for 10x the data; the other engines of the project grow 6–10x). Worst queries (1m -> 10m median): q01_filter_selective 0.05 -> 27.3 ms, q05_groupby_low_card 1.6 -> 41.5 ms, q16_timeseries_hourly 0.8 -> 22.0 ms, q14_sort_full_string 15.4 -> 411 ms, q12_left_join_anti 6.7 -> 183 ms, q10_join_customers 7.1 -> 188 ms. HTTP throughput (`serve`, transactions and customers loaded, q01/q03/q05/q09) falls from 190–232 qps at 16 clients (1m) to 17 qps (10m); single-client median latency 18 ms -> 160 ms. Black-box observations of the engine process at 10m, none of which occur at 1m: (1) the latency the client sees is much larger than the engine's own `stats.elapsed_us`: q01 27.3 ms wall vs 0.05 ms reported, and about 365 ms of the 2,220 ms per round lie outside the reported time (at 1m the difference is below 0.15 ms per query); (2) a query's latency depends on what ran before it in the session: in a fresh session with all 10m tables loaded q01 takes 0.03 ms, q05 12.9 ms, q16 1.7 ms, q17 0.9 ms, but 21, 22, 4.6 and 20.8 ms in the interleaved benchmark order; (3) per round of the 20 queries the process takes about 2.1 million minor page faults and 4.6 s of system CPU (q15 496k faults, q14 415k, q10 188k, q07 151k; repeating one query back to back still faults every time), versus 54 minor faults and no measurable system CPU per round at 1m. Single-threaded operator time grows about linearly (q02 with `threads: 1`: 15 ms -> 155 ms). Find and remove the causes of the super-linear growth (session mode first; HTTP mode too if you can) without changing any result. Reproduce: `python3 datasets/generators/pqgen.py generate --scale 10m --jobs 8` and the same with `--scale 1m` (use `--jobs 1` if multiprocessing fails; output goes to the git-ignored `datasets/generated/`, about 2 GB for 10m), then `python3 benchmarks/harness/bench.py --engines {{LANG_DIR}} --scale 10m --no-sandbox --cpus '' --mem-limit-gb 0 --label <name>` (you are already inside a sandbox; add `--http` for the throughput part, `--queries q01,q05` for a subset, `--reps`/`--warmup` to shorten). It writes `results/performance/<id>/summary.json` (per-query `latency_seconds` medians and result `digests`) and `raw.jsonl.gz` (per execution incl. `engine_elapsed_us`). A full 10m run of this engine takes several minutes; the host has 32 logical CPUs and over 200 GB of RAM, and the engine's peak RSS at 10m is about 12 GB.
optimize-scaling.done: README.md contains a before/after table (bench.py medians of all 20 queries plus the geometric mean, at 10m and at 1m, same host and settings, measured back to back) and a short explanation of the causes found and the change; the 10m geometric mean improves measurably, no query gets slower at 1m beyond measurement noise, and every query's result digest at 1m and at 10m is identical before and after; peak RSS at 10m does not grow by more than about 25 %. All public checks still pass: `python3 tests/conformance/runner.py --engine implementations/{{LANG_DIR}}/bin/polyquery`, the same with `--modes` and with `--transport http`, `python3 tests/concurrency/http_suite.py --engine implementations/{{LANG_DIR}}/bin/polyquery` and `python3 tests/regression/robustness_probe.py --engine implementations/{{LANG_DIR}}/bin/polyquery --only expression_limits --require-pass` (0 failures, 0 errors, 0 not-implemented except optionally correlated subqueries); the capability set is unchanged; `make build test` succeed; generated data and benchmark results are not committed; all work is committed.

app-pqledger.title: Embedding API and the pqledger application
app-pqledger.goal: Application and library task (identical for every language): your accepted engine (Phases 1–5 and all later changes) is in `implementations/{{LANG_DIR}}/`. (1) Make the engine usable as a library from {{LANGUAGE}} programs: expose the embedding API specified in `spec/apps/embedding.md` (create an instance, load, query with typed result values, save/open, drop/list/schema, close; errors carrying the specification's error codes) and package it in the language's usual form (§2). (2) Build `pqledger`, the personal-finance command-line application specified in `spec/apps/pqledger.md`, on that API: importing bank-statement CSV exports in configurable formats, duplicate detection, rule-based categories, reports, budgets, ad-hoc SQL and three output formats, with the ledger stored as PQCF files that any other implementation can read. (3) Write the minimal embedding example `examples/embed-demo` (embedding.md §5).
